# Forensic Dossier — ALHG.PA (Louis Hachette Group S.A.)

**CRITICAL IDENTITY CORRECTION:** The screener/peer file labels ALHG.PA as "Albin Michel, a French trade book publisher." This is **wrong**. ALHG.PA is **Louis Hachette Group S.A. (LHG)** — a Bolloré-controlled holding company spun out of Vivendi in October 2024 and listed on Euronext Growth Paris on 16 December 2024. LHG owns **66.53% of Lagardère SA** (which itself houses Lagardère Publishing = Hachette Livre, and Lagardère Travel Retail) plus **100% of Prisma Media**. This is not a thin single-line book publisher; it is a three-segment, €9.6bn-revenue media/travel-retail conglomerate held through a holdco structure. Every downstream number — the €9.23B→€9.62B revenue jump, the multi-billion net debt, the 0.2% net margin — is explained by full consolidation of Lagardère, NOT by a book publisher. The entire peer-group rationale ("structurally thin economics of physical book publishing," Altman-Z distress) is built on a misidentified company and must be discarded.

No FMP transcript was bundled. This dossier is built from the FY2025 results press release and earnings call (reported 19 Feb 2026), the Prisma transaction release (closed 31 Mar 2026), the H1-2025 release, Lagardère SA disclosures, and the Vivendi/Lagardère litigation record — all web-sourced and dated below.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

LHG's story since its Dec-2024 listing has been a **deleveraging-and-simplification** narrative wrapped around a cyclical recovery in two strong operating businesses. At listing the pitch was "a leading, diversified player in publishing, travel retail and media" — a holdco housing Lagardère's two crown jewels (Hachette Livre, the world's #3 trade publisher; Lagardère Travel Retail, the global #2 airport/travel concessionaire) plus a structurally-declining magazine asset (Prisma).

By FY2025 the emphasis had visibly **shifted from "diversified holdco" to "deleverage + clean up the portfolio."** Management foregrounded: (i) net-debt reduction of €236M to €1,590M and leverage down from 2.4x to 1.95x; (ii) the Prisma luxury-division disposal and Vivendi's 13.58% Prisma-holding-stake purchase, framed by Arnaud Lagardère as "refocus[ing] its portfolio on its core historical businesses"; (iii) Travel Retail's record EBITDA (€312M, +17%) and the Schiphol duty-free contract takeover. The growth driver that was quietly *contained* rather than dropped is Prisma — repeatedly described in defensive, restructuring language ("downturn in business," "rapidly changing market," ~300 jobs cut across two plans, −€43M EBITDA). The arc is therefore **stabilizing/strengthening at the group level** (deleverage on track, two healthy segments) with one segment in managed decline.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Mgmt claim (FY2025 call, 19 Feb 2026) | Hard evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Revenue €9.6bn, +4% reported / +3.3% LfL" | Screener: rev €9.62B vs €9.23B FY24 = +4.2% YoY. 3-yr "CAGR +210.9%" is a **demerger/consolidation artifact** (2023 showed €979M as a stub; full Lagardère consolidation lands in FY24). True organic run-rate ≈ +3–4%. | **MATCH** — and confirms the 210% CAGR is noise, not acceleration. |

Both real; the SoP must use consolidated EV but credit the deleveraging trajectory. | **RECONCILED** — the gap is consolidation scope, not a hidden liability. **In any SoP, net debt is a LIABILITY to subtract.** |
| Travel Retail "record EBITDA €312M, +17%; 5.1% op margin; Schiphol takeover seamless" | Consistent with Lagardère SA's own FY25 (Travel Retail rev +5.5% to €6,133M). Genuine post-COVID travel recovery. | **MATCH** — strongest part of the story. |

The narrative is **honestly poorer than the holdco optics suggest and honestly richer than the screener's "0.2% net margin / Altman-Z distress" optics suggest** — both distortions cancel once you see the consolidation structure.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising/Stable.** As a freshly-listed holdco there are only ~2-3 reporting cycles, but the trajectory across H1-2025 → FY2025 is one of **growing specificity and confidence on deleverage and Travel Retail**, paired with **increasingly defensive, surgical language on Prisma.** FY25 management was concrete: named leverage targets (1.95x → continued de-gearing), specific refinancing (€500M 5-yr bond oversubscribed 3x + €300M private placement, WAM 2.9 yrs), and forward guidance ("stable 2026 publishing revenue," "mid-single-digit travel-retail growth," margins consistent). The shift from offensive (growth/M&A) to defensive (cost/restructuring) language is **isolated to Prisma**, not the group. Net: confidence **Stable-to-Rising**, with management demonstrably willing to give dated, falsifiable guidance.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-High, but short track record.** LHG has guided only a handful of times since listing; FY2025 delivered the deleveraging it promised at H1 (net debt down €236M, leverage 2.4x→1.95x — concrete and verifiable). Travel Retail hit "record" numbers consistent with parent Lagardère's disclosures. There is **no multi-year history to test for sandbagging**, and the attributable-EPS line is so thin and minority-diluted that small swings look large (latest-Q EPS YoY −70% on the screener is noise on a near-zero base, not a miss). Reliability: **Medium** (would be High with another 2-3 cycles). The credibility risk is **not** management honesty on operations — it is the **governance/control overhang** (see §5, §6) that sits *above* the operating story.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring, unresolved questions are not operational — they are **structural/governance**:
1. **The holdco discount & simplification path.** LHG trades at a discount to its look-through NAV (66.53% of Lagardère ≈ €1.85–1.97bn at Lagardère's ~€2.96bn cap, plus 100% of Prisma, vs LHG's own ~€1.2bn market cap). Analysts press on whether/when the two-tier Lagardère/LHG structure collapses (merger, buy-in of Lagardère minorities, or a simplified single listing). Management has **not committed to a timeline** — this is the load-bearing, unanswered question.
2. **The Vivendi-demerger legal cloud.** Analysts probe the AMF/court overhang: the Paris Court of Appeal (Apr-2025) found the Bolloré family exercised effective control and ordered the AMF to reconsider whether a **mandatory buyout offer** was owed at the Vivendi split; separately the EU gun-jumping probe into Vivendi/Lagardère went against the companies at the General Court (3 Jun 2026), with Vivendi appealing to the CJEU. Management deflects these as Vivendi/parent matters.
3. **Prisma's terminal value.** Analysts keep returning to whether Prisma is a permanent EBITDA drag; management's answer is disposals + digital/AI pivot, not a fix.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 **Deleveraging is real and on-track** (net debt −€236M, 2.4x→1.95x; €800M refinanced, WAM 2.9 yrs, no near-term maturity wall) — the Altman-Z "1.1 distress" flag is a **false positive** driven by consolidating low-margin travel-retail revenue against gross debt; it does not reflect refinancing risk.
🟢 **Two genuinely good operating assets** — Lagardère Travel Retail (global #2, record EBITDA, structural post-COVID tailwind) and Hachette Livre (world #3 trade publisher, share-gaining).
🟢 **First dividend initiated** (€0.06) — a capital-return signal, not a cut.
🟢 **Portfolio clean-up underway** — Prisma luxury sale closed, non-core trimmed.
🔴 **Holdco-on-holdco structure** — value leaks twice (LHG → Lagardère minorities → operating subs); 33.5% of the best assets accrues to MMB.PA holders, not ALHG.
🔴 **Governance/control overhang** — Bolloré 31% control + Arnaud Lagardère's contested position + the AMF mandatory-buyout question + EU gun-jumping appeal = an open-ended legal/governance binary the equity cannot dictate.
🔴 **Prisma is a structurally shrinking, loss-making segment** (rev −9% to €266M, EBITDA −€43M) in the cord-cutting/print-decline tail.
🔴 **Euronext Growth listing, thin float optics** — minority equity in a controlled vehicle; the controller, not the market, sets the simplification clock.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The language migration around Prisma — from "media" to "refocus on core historical businesses," "digital transformation," "generative AI" — is the standard euphemism arc for **managing a melting asset toward disposal**, not investing into it. Watch for a full Prisma exit.
- The Vivendi 13.58%-of-Prisma-holding purchase is a **related-party tell**: it monetizes a sliver of Prisma to a Bolloré-affiliated counterparty (Vivendi) and hints the controller may *recombine* assets across the Bolloré complex over time — a double-edged signal for minorities (could simplify *or* could be done on terms favoring the controller).
- Management's repeated emphasis on **covenant leverage (1.95x)** rather than consolidated gross debt is a deliberate framing to steer analysts away from the headline €4.5bn consolidated figure — legitimate, but a framing choice worth noting.
- The €500M bond **oversubscribed 3x** is a real credit-market vote of confidence that contradicts the screener's distress flag.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE → STRENGTHENING at the operating level; the *equity* story is a CONTROLLED HOLDCO-DISCOUNT special-situation whose resolution clock is held by the Bolloré family, not the market.**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a holdco-discount/sum-of-parts trade, not an operating-momentum trade — and the catalyst that would close the discount (structural simplification / Lagardère minority buy-in / a single clean listing) is UNANNOUNCED, controller-discretionary, and entangled with active Vivendi/AMF/EU litigation.** The underlying assets (Travel Retail #2, Hachette #3) are real and deleveraging is genuine, so the *downside* is cushioned by tangible NAV; but the *upside* requires a corporate-action the minority cannot force, on a timeline the controller will set to suit itself. Size as a patient, asset-backed, low-conviction-on-timing position — never as a dated-catalyst bet.

**ECONOMIC MOAT:** Lagardère Travel Retail has a genuine **regulatory-license / scale-cost concession moat** (long-dated airport contracts, global #2 scale, switching costs to airport authorities) — NARROW-to-decent and currently *widening* (record EBITDA, Schiphol win). Hachette Livre has an **intangible-brand/backlist** moat (Astérix, Twilight, frontlist relationships) — NARROW and roughly stable in a flat print market. Prisma has **no moat** and is structurally impaired. Blended at the group level: **NARROW**, trend **STABLE** (Travel-Retail widening offsets Prisma erosion). This is not a high-but-falling-ROIC eroding-moat situation; group ROIC is *low-but-recovering* off the COVID trough, which is different.

**SECULAR THREAT:** The print/magazine secular decline (cord-cutting/print) is **terminal for Prisma but Prisma is only ~3% of revenue and already loss-making/being disposed** — so at the group level the secular threat is **MANAGEABLE**, not terminal. Travel Retail (60%+ of revenue) is a post-COVID *recovery* asset with a structural travel-growth tailwind, the opposite of a secular loser. The cheapness here is therefore best read as a **holdco-discount + governance-overhang fear-print on sound assets**, NOT a structurally-shrinking base — i.e. closer to mispricing than value trap, gated by the absence of a forcing catalyst.

# Louis Hachette Group (ALHG.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*A deep dive on the company, the setup, and management credibility. No bundled earnings-call transcript was available; this dossier is built from the company's Full-Year 2025 results (published 19 February 2026), the FY2025 investor slides, the 2026 shareholders' meeting materials, the AMF and Cour de Cassation filings on the Vivendi control case, and live market data as of early July 2026. Where a claim rests on management's own words, it is drawn from the results release, not a call recording.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Louis Hachette Group is not an operating company in the usual sense. It is a holding vehicle — a company whose main asset is a controlling stake in another listed company. It was carved out of Vivendi in December 2024, when Vivendi split itself into four pieces (Canal+, Havas, Louis Hachette Group, and a rump Vivendi). Louis Hachette Group was handed two things: a 66.53% controlling stake in Lagardère S.A. (itself listed in Paris under ticker MMB), and 100% of Prisma Media, a French magazine publisher. It began trading on Euronext Growth Paris on 16 December 2024 at €1.12 per share.

The story here has barely had time to "evolve" — the company is only about eighteen months old as a public entity. But the arc that matters is the one it inherited. Lagardère runs two good businesses: Lagardère Publishing (Hachette Livre — one of the world's largest trade-book publishers) and Lagardère Travel Retail (the Relay newsstands, duty-free, and food-and-beverage concessions you walk past in airports and train stations). Bolted onto the holding company is Prisma Media, a declining print-magazine business. And sitting over the whole structure is Vincent Bolloré, the French industrialist, who controls Louis Hachette Group with a 30.4% stake and is the ultimate architect of the entire Vivendi break-up.

The narrative, then, is a classic holding-company-discount setup: a listed holding company that trades for less than the market value of the listed stake it owns.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The screener's raw metrics for this name are badly distorted by the consolidation, and a careful reader must correct them before drawing any conclusion. Because Louis Hachette Group consolidates 100% of Lagardère's revenue and debt onto its own accounts (it controls Lagardère, so accounting rules make it book the whole thing), the headline figures describe Lagardère's business, not the value that flows to a Louis Hachette shareholder.

| Management / reported claim (FY2025, released 19 Feb 2026) | The hard number | Verdict |

| "Revenue rose to €9.6 billion, up 4.2% reported" | €9.62B, +4.2% — matches the screener's €9.62B | Verified. This is Lagardère's consolidated top line, not Louis Hachette's own. |

| "Leverage improved to 1.95x" (net debt divided by a cash-earnings measure) | Net debt €1,590M, down €236M | Verified — and this flatly contradicts the screener's "net debt 4.49B." Use €1.59B. |
| "Strong cash generation, CFFO up 9% to €558M" | €558M cash flow from operations; cash flow after interest and tax €363M, up 39% | Verified; the cash story is real and improving. |
| Net income, group share | Only €22M | This is the tell. On €9.6B of revenue, the profit that actually belongs to Louis Hachette shareholders is a rounding error — because Louis Hachette only owns two-thirds of Lagardère, and Lagardère's own net margin is thin. The screener's "Net 0.2%" margin is therefore accurate but misleading: it reflects a leveraged, low-margin, minority-diluted structure, not a broken business. |

**Segment reality (FY2025):**
- Lagardère Publishing: revenue €3,001M (+4.5% reported), EBITA €308M (+6.6%). A healthy ~10% margin, growing. The crown jewel.
- Lagardère Travel Retail: revenue €6,133M (+5.5% reported), record year, strong gains in Europe, Africa, and South America. The scale engine; thinner margins but recovering post-pandemic.
- Lagardère Live (events/broadcasting): revenue €219M, EBITA −€20M. Small, loss-making, recovering.
- Prisma Media: revenue €266M, down about 10% like-for-like, EBITA −€43M. A structurally declining magazine business and a real drag.

The screener's "3-yr revenue CAGR +210.9%" and "net income CAGR" figures are artefacts of the 2024 consolidation event (revenue jumped from €979M to €9.23B the year Lagardère was consolidated), not organic growth. Ignore them entirely.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

*No earnings-call transcript was available, so tone can only be read from the written releases.* The written commentary is confident and operationally focused: management leads with revenue and profit growth, emphasizes debt reduction ("allowing the Group to continue reducing its debt"), and frames 2025 as a year of both growth and deleveraging. Trajectory: Stable-to-Rising on the operating businesses, with the important caveat that the written record cannot reveal the hedging and deflection a live call would.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

With only about eighteen months of public history and no multi-quarter guidance track record to test, a full credibility scorecard cannot be built. What can be said: the FY2025 results delivered on the twin promises visible since listing — grow the two Lagardère franchises and cut debt — and both happened (EBITA +8%, net debt −€236M, leverage 2.4x → 1.95x). That is a clean first full year. Reliability: provisionally Medium, pending a longer record.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The unresolved question that hangs over every conversation about this name is governance, not operations. Two threads:

1. **The Vivendi control case.** A Paris appellate court found in April 2025 that Vincent Bolloré exercised de facto control over Vivendi, which — had it stood — could have forced a mandatory buyout of Vivendi's (and by extension the spin-offs') minority holders. On 28 November 2025 the Cour de Cassation (France's top court) overturned that finding and sent the case back to a differently composed appeals court. The AMF (the French market regulator) has said it cannot rule on any mandatory-bid obligation until the appeals court rules again. So the single largest potential catalyst — a forced take-out at a premium — is live but unresolved and not currently required.
2. **The holding-company discount.** Analysts repeatedly probe why Louis Hachette should trade below the value of its Lagardère stake, and whether Bolloré intends to simplify the structure (collapse the Louis Hachette / Lagardère double-listing) — which would be the cleanest way to close the gap.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Governance overhang: a controlling shareholder (Bolloré, 30.4%) with a long history of squeezing minorities cheaply; the minority holder's interests and the controller's are not automatically aligned.
🔴 Prisma Media is a structurally shrinking print-magazine asset (−10% like-for-like, loss-making) — a slow value leak.
🔴 A double holding-company layer (Louis Hachette over Lagardère over the operating businesses) means two sets of minority discounts and complexity.
🔴 The screener's distress signals (Altman-Z ~1.1) are consolidation artefacts, but the genuine leverage — €1.59B net debt plus large lease obligations at travel retail — is real and cyclical.

🟢 Both core businesses grew revenue and profit in 2025; travel retail hit a record.
🟢 Debt fell and leverage improved to 1.95x — the balance sheet is moving the right way.
🟢 The company trades below the market value of just its listed 66.53% Lagardère stake, so a buyer effectively gets Prisma Media and any structure-simplification upside for free.
🟢 A dividend was initiated with a clear pass-through policy (≥85% of dividends received).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling signal is structural, not verbal. Bolloré assembled this exact double-decker — Louis Hachette owning a controlling-but-not-total stake in a separately listed Lagardère — deliberately, out of the Vivendi break-up. Bolloré's playbook across his career (Vivendi itself, Compagnie de l'Odet, earlier Bolloré-group reorganizations) has repeatedly been to simplify multi-layered structures at moments of his choosing, usually on terms favorable to the controller. A minority investor here is, in effect, betting alongside — or against — Bolloré's eventual intentions. That is the whole game.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The underlying businesses are growing modestly and de-levering; there is no operating crisis and no operating boom. This is a value/holding-company-discount situation, not a growth or turnaround story.

It could be years, or it could be never on favorable terms.

**Economic moat:** The value ultimately rests on Lagardère Publishing (Hachette Livre), which has a genuine intangible-brand-and-backlist moat — a narrow but real moat in trade publishing, one of the more durable niches in media. Travel retail is a scale-and-concession business with contract-based positions but no wide moat. The blended franchise is **NARROW** and **STABLE** — returns are modest but not eroding; there is no evidence of a collapsing return profile in the core.

**Secular threat:** Manageable. Trade-book publishing has proved unusually resilient to digital disruption (physical books endure; audiobooks add growth), and airport/travel retail is a structural-growth channel tied to global passenger traffic. The one genuinely secularly-challenged piece — Prisma Media's print magazines — is small (about 3% of revenue). There is no terminal-value threat to the core.

# Forensic Dossier — Louis Hachette Group S.A. (ALHG.PA)

*A deep dive on the setup. Prepared for the investment committee, 11 July 2026. Live price €1.764 on Euronext Paris (market value about €1.75 billion). Signal type: deep value.*

**Evidence note.** Louis Hachette Group ("LHG") is a young company — it was carved out of Vivendi and listed on 16 December 2024, so it has only one full year of stand-alone reporting. No earnings-call transcripts are available for it (the paid data feed returns none, and the company does not host quarterly analyst calls in the U.S. style). This dossier therefore tests the *published financial record* — the 2024 and 2025 annual results, the segment disclosures, and the dated court ruling of 8 July 2026 — rather than management's spoken words. Where a transcript would normally supply tone and guidance-tracking, that evidence is simply absent, and I say so rather than invent it.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story here is unusually clean because the company is essentially a *holding vehicle*. Louis Hachette Group owns two things: a controlling **66.29% stake in Lagardère SA** (the publishing-and-travel-retail group, itself listed in Paris under MMB.PA) and **100% of Prisma Media** (a French magazine publisher). It has almost no operations of its own — the profile literally describes it as a company whose "strategic vision involves establishing publishing and travel retail operations … through its various subsidiaries." So the narrative is not really LHG's; it is Lagardère's, plus a corporate-structure overlay inherited from the 2024 break-up of Vivendi.

The arc since listing has had two threads:

- **The operating thread (improving).** Lagardère has delivered a genuine post-pandemic recovery. Group revenue climbed from roughly €0.98 billion in 2023 (a figure that pre-dates full consolidation of Lagardère) to €9.23 billion in 2024 and €9.62 billion in 2025 as reported at the LHG level. Recurring operating profit (recurring EBIT — the profit from normal operations before one-offs) at Lagardère reached €641 million in 2025, up 8%, and the balance sheet de-levered from 2.4× to 1.95× net-debt-to-earnings. This is the part of the story that has strengthened.

- **The corporate-structure thread (now resolved against the bulls).** The reason a special-situations investor looked at LHG at all was a lawsuit. A minority Vivendi shareholder, CIAM, argued that Vincent Bolloré — who controls the Bolloré group and retained 29.3% of Vivendi after the 2024 split — in fact *controlled* Vivendi, which under French law would have forced him to launch a mandatory buyout of the whole complex at a fair price. That would have dragged the deliberately-cheap spin-offs (Canal+, Havas, and Louis Hachette Group) back up toward undistorted value. On **8 July 2026 the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Bolloré does not control Vivendi**, removing that forced-bid path. This thread, which was the entire reason to expect a near-term re-rating, has now closed unfavourably.

## 2. Claims vs financials (forensic)

Because there is no transcript, I test the company's *published* claims against its own numbers.

| Management/company claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record financial results driven by all businesses in 2025" (Lagardère FY2025 release) | Revenue +4.6% reported / +3.8% like-for-like; recurring EBIT €641m (+8%); Publishing recurring EBIT €312m; Travel Retail €334m (+9.5%). | **Holds** for the two core businesses. |
| "All businesses contributing to growth" | Not quite. **Prisma Media revenue fell to €266m (−10% like-for-like) and its EBITA swung to −€43m from +€13m**, hit by restructuring; Lagardère Live (live entertainment) also lost about €20m. | **Overstated** — two smaller units are loss-making. |
| Steady de-leveraging | Net debt (excluding leases) fell €236m to €1,590m; leverage 2.4× → 1.95×; cash flow after interest and tax up 39% to €363m. | **Holds** — delivered as advertised. |
| The stock is worth more than its parts | The 66.29% Lagardère stake alone is worth about €1.89 billion at Lagardère's market price, against LHG's own €1.75 billion market value — so the shares trade *below* the quoted value of just the controlling stake, before counting Prisma. | **Holds directionally**, but the gap is modest (see §8). |

The honest read: the *core* narrative (a recovering, de-levering publishing-and-travel-retail group trading below the market value of the stake that holds it) is corroborated by the numbers. The *embellishment* ("all businesses growing") is not — Prisma is shrinking and now loss-making, and it is being restructured, with its luxury division sold and Vivendi taking a stake in the remaining Prisma entity.

## 3. Tone & confidence trajectory

No transcripts exist, so tone must be read from actions rather than words. The revealed posture is **cautiously offensive on the core, defensive on the periphery**: the company kept investing in travel-retail concessions and publishing while cutting and reshaping the weak magazine unit (restructuring charges, luxury-division disposal, a partner brought into Prisma). Initiating a dividend (€0.06 per share for 2025) is a confidence signal — a newly-listed holding company does not start paying out cash unless it believes the underlying cash flows are durable. Rating: **stable**, leaning constructive on operations.

## 4. Guidance credibility

LHG does not issue formal quantitative guidance in the manner of a U.S. company, so there is no multi-quarter guide-versus-deliver record to score. What can be checked is the de-leveraging trajectory management pointed to at listing: it targeted continued balance-sheet repair and delivered it (2.4× → 1.95×, net debt down €236m). Against that, the one place where the implicit "all businesses recovering" framing did not deliver was Prisma. On the evidence available: **reliability medium-to-high on the balance sheet and core operations; the promotional gloss on the weak units is the soft spot.**

## 5. Analyst pressure points

The recurring worry an outside analyst returns to is not operational — it is **structural and governance-driven**. Three questions dominate and management cannot fully answer any of them, because the answers sit with Vincent Bolloré, not with LHG:

- Will the holding-company discount ever close, given that *every* Bolloré-controlled vehicle (Bolloré SE, Vivendi, Canal+, Havas) trades at a persistent discount to the value of what it owns?
- What is Bolloré's end-game — a patient mop-up of minorities at a low price, or leaving the structure discounted indefinitely?
- Now that the 8 July court ruling has removed the forced-bid lever, what *else* could force the value out?

The consensus price target (about €2.33) sits well above the current €1.76, which tells you analysts credit the full look-through value — but they have no dated mechanism to realise it.

## 6. Red flags / green flags

🟢 De-leveraging delivered (2.4× → 1.95×), and cash flow after interest and tax up 39% — real, not cosmetic.
🟢 Core segments growing: Publishing recurring EBIT €312m, Travel Retail €334m (+9.5%).
🟢 Dividend initiated (€0.06/share) — a durability signal from a brand-new listing.
🟢 The shares trade below the market value of the 66.29% Lagardère stake alone.

🔴 **The load-bearing catalyst fired against the thesis on 8 July 2026** — the Paris Court of Appeal ruled Bolloré does not control Vivendi, killing the near-term forced-bid path. CIAM will appeal to the Cour de cassation, but that court already remanded the case once, and the path is long and uncertain.
🔴 Prisma Media is now loss-making (−€43m EBITA) and shrinking (−10% like-for-like), mid-restructuring.
🔴 It is a **Bolloré-controlled holding company** — the discount is structural, and control means minority holders cannot force a value-crystallising event.
🔴 The stock is near its 52-week high (€1.83) and never sold off on the ruling — so there is no wash-out to buy, and no cheap entry has been handed to us.

## 7. Hidden signals

The most telling signal is what *did not* happen: when the court ruling landed and Vivendi fell about 10%, **Louis Hachette Group did not drop** — it is trading up on the day and near its highs. That reveals the market never actually priced a takeover premium into LHG; the forced-bid optionality lived in Vivendi's shares, not here. So the ruling, while it kills the special-situation *narrative*, does little to LHG's *price*. The second quiet signal is the Prisma reshaping — selling the luxury titles and bringing Vivendi in as a Prisma shareholder looks like the first step toward tidying the magazine unit out of the story, which would leave LHG as a cleaner proxy for the Lagardère stake over time.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a recovering, de-levering, controlled holding company whose core businesses are growing and whose weak periphery is being cut — but whose one hard, dated catalyst has now resolved unfavourably.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the reason this was a *special situation* — a court-ordered forced bid that would drag the cheap spin-offs up to fair value — died on 8 July 2026. What remains is an ordinary holding-company-discount trade: the shares sit about 8% below the market value of just the Lagardère stake, and roughly 14% below a full look-through value that also credits (a now loss-making) Prisma. That discount is real but *structurally sticky*, because Bolloré-controlled vehicles trade at persistent discounts and control removes any mechanism for minorities to force closure. With the stock near its highs and no forcing function left, the honest classification is dead-money-with-asset-backing, not asymmetric upside.

**Economic moat.** The durable earnings sit inside Lagardère. Publishing (Hachette Livre — the world's third-largest trade-book publisher) has an intangible-brand and backlist moat that is real but narrow; travel retail has scale in airport concessions, but returns are competed away at each concession renewal, so that too is narrow. Group returns on capital look optically low (weighed down by goodwill and lease accounting), but the underlying franchises earn steady, mid-single-digit-growing profits. **Moat: narrow; trend: stable** — recurring profit is rising and margins are steady-to-improving, so this is not an eroding franchise.

**Secular threat.** Manageable, not terminal. Trade-book publishing carries some long-run exposure to generative-AI and e-book substitution, but physical trade books have proven resilient and Hachette's backlist is an asset, not a liability. Travel retail grows structurally with air passenger traffic. Neither business faces a melting terminal value. The cheapness here is a *governance/holding-company discount*, not a fear-print on a shrinking base — which is why it is a fair-value trade rather than either a screaming bargain or a value trap.

# Forensic Dossier — Louis Hachette Group S.A. (ALHG.PA)

*A deep dive on the setup. Prepared for the investment committee, 11 July 2026. Live price €1.764 on Euronext Paris (market value about €1.75 billion). Signal type: deep value.*

**Evidence note.** Louis Hachette Group ("LHG") is a young company — it was carved out of Vivendi and listed on 16 December 2024, so it has only one full year of stand-alone reporting. No earnings-call transcripts are available for it (the paid data feed returns none, and the company does not host quarterly analyst calls in the U.S. style). This dossier therefore tests the *published financial record* — the 2024 and 2025 annual results, the segment disclosures, and the dated court ruling of 8 July 2026 — rather than management's spoken words. Where a transcript would normally supply tone and guidance-tracking, that evidence is simply absent, and I say so rather than invent it.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story here is unusually clean because the company is essentially a *holding vehicle*. Louis Hachette Group owns two things: a controlling **66.29% stake in Lagardère SA** (the publishing-and-travel-retail group, itself listed in Paris under MMB.PA) and **100% of Prisma Media** (a French magazine publisher). It has almost no operations of its own — the profile literally describes it as a company whose "strategic vision involves establishing publishing and travel retail operations … through its various subsidiaries." So the narrative is not really LHG's; it is Lagardère's, plus a corporate-structure overlay inherited from the 2024 break-up of Vivendi.

The arc since listing has had two threads:

- **The operating thread (improving).** Lagardère has delivered a genuine post-pandemic recovery. Group revenue climbed from roughly €0.98 billion in 2023 (a figure that pre-dates full consolidation of Lagardère) to €9.23 billion in 2024 and €9.62 billion in 2025 as reported at the LHG level. Recurring operating profit (recurring EBIT — the profit from normal operations before one-offs) at Lagardère reached €641 million in 2025, up 8%, and the balance sheet de-levered from 2.4× to 1.95× net-debt-to-earnings. This is the part of the story that has strengthened.

- **The corporate-structure thread (now resolved against the bulls).** The reason a special-situations investor looked at LHG at all was a lawsuit. A minority Vivendi shareholder, CIAM, argued that Vincent Bolloré — who controls the Bolloré group and retained 29.3% of Vivendi after the 2024 split — in fact *controlled* Vivendi, which under French law would have forced him to launch a mandatory buyout of the whole complex at a fair price. That would have dragged the deliberately-cheap spin-offs (Canal+, Havas, and Louis Hachette Group) back up toward undistorted value. On **8 July 2026 the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Bolloré does not control Vivendi**, removing that forced-bid path. This thread, which was the entire reason to expect a near-term re-rating, has now closed unfavourably.

## 2. Claims vs financials (forensic)

Because there is no transcript, I test the company's *published* claims against its own numbers.

| Management/company claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record financial results driven by all businesses in 2025" (Lagardère FY2025 release) | Revenue +4.6% reported / +3.8% like-for-like; recurring EBIT €641m (+8%); Publishing recurring EBIT €312m; Travel Retail €334m (+9.5%). | **Holds** for the two core businesses. |
| "All businesses contributing to growth" | Not quite. **Prisma Media revenue fell to €266m (−10% like-for-like) and its EBITA swung to −€43m from +€13m**, hit by restructuring; Lagardère Live (live entertainment) also lost about €20m. | **Overstated** — two smaller units are loss-making. |
| Steady de-leveraging | Net debt (excluding leases) fell €236m to €1,590m; leverage 2.4× → 1.95×; cash flow after interest and tax up 39% to €363m. | **Holds** — delivered as advertised. |
| The stock is worth more than its parts | The 66.29% Lagardère stake alone is worth about €1.89 billion at Lagardère's market price, against LHG's own €1.75 billion market value — so the shares trade *below* the quoted value of just the controlling stake, before counting Prisma. | **Holds directionally**, but the gap is modest (see §8). |

The honest read: the *core* narrative (a recovering, de-levering publishing-and-travel-retail group trading below the market value of the stake that holds it) is corroborated by the numbers. The *embellishment* ("all businesses growing") is not — Prisma is shrinking and now loss-making, and it is being restructured, with its luxury division sold and Vivendi taking a stake in the remaining Prisma entity.

## 3. Tone & confidence trajectory

No transcripts exist, so tone must be read from actions rather than words. The revealed posture is **cautiously offensive on the core, defensive on the periphery**: the company kept investing in travel-retail concessions and publishing while cutting and reshaping the weak magazine unit (restructuring charges, luxury-division disposal, a partner brought into Prisma). Initiating a dividend (€0.06 per share for 2025) is a confidence signal — a newly-listed holding company does not start paying out cash unless it believes the underlying cash flows are durable. Rating: **stable**, leaning constructive on operations.

## 4. Guidance credibility

LHG does not issue formal quantitative guidance in the manner of a U.S. company, so there is no multi-quarter guide-versus-deliver record to score. What can be checked is the de-leveraging trajectory management pointed to at listing: it targeted continued balance-sheet repair and delivered it (2.4× → 1.95×, net debt down €236m). Against that, the one place where the implicit "all businesses recovering" framing did not deliver was Prisma. On the evidence available: **reliability medium-to-high on the balance sheet and core operations; the promotional gloss on the weak units is the soft spot.**

## 5. Analyst pressure points

The recurring worry an outside analyst returns to is not operational — it is **structural and governance-driven**. Three questions dominate and management cannot fully answer any of them, because the answers sit with Vincent Bolloré, not with LHG:

- Will the holding-company discount ever close, given that *every* Bolloré-controlled vehicle (Bolloré SE, Vivendi, Canal+, Havas) trades at a persistent discount to the value of what it owns?
- What is Bolloré's end-game — a patient mop-up of minorities at a low price, or leaving the structure discounted indefinitely?
- Now that the 8 July court ruling has removed the forced-bid lever, what *else* could force the value out?

The consensus price target (about €2.33) sits well above the current €1.76, which tells you analysts credit the full look-through value — but they have no dated mechanism to realise it.

## 6. Red flags / green flags

🟢 De-leveraging delivered (2.4× → 1.95×), and cash flow after interest and tax up 39% — real, not cosmetic.
🟢 Core segments growing: Publishing recurring EBIT €312m, Travel Retail €334m (+9.5%).
🟢 Dividend initiated (€0.06/share) — a durability signal from a brand-new listing.
🟢 The shares trade below the market value of the 66.29% Lagardère stake alone.

🔴 **The load-bearing catalyst fired against the thesis on 8 July 2026** — the Paris Court of Appeal ruled Bolloré does not control Vivendi, killing the near-term forced-bid path. CIAM will appeal to the Cour de cassation, but that court already remanded the case once, and the path is long and uncertain.
🔴 Prisma Media is now loss-making (−€43m EBITA) and shrinking (−10% like-for-like), mid-restructuring.
🔴 It is a **Bolloré-controlled holding company** — the discount is structural, and control means minority holders cannot force a value-crystallising event.
🔴 The stock is near its 52-week high (€1.83) and never sold off on the ruling — so there is no wash-out to buy, and no cheap entry has been handed to us.

## 7. Hidden signals

The most telling signal is what *did not* happen: when the court ruling landed and Vivendi fell about 10%, **Louis Hachette Group did not drop** — it is trading up on the day and near its highs. That reveals the market never actually priced a takeover premium into LHG; the forced-bid optionality lived in Vivendi's shares, not here. So the ruling, while it kills the special-situation *narrative*, does little to LHG's *price*. The second quiet signal is the Prisma reshaping — selling the luxury titles and bringing Vivendi in as a Prisma shareholder looks like the first step toward tidying the magazine unit out of the story, which would leave LHG as a cleaner proxy for the Lagardère stake over time.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a recovering, de-levering, controlled holding company whose core businesses are growing and whose weak periphery is being cut — but whose one hard, dated catalyst has now resolved unfavourably.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the reason this was a *special situation* — a court-ordered forced bid that would drag the cheap spin-offs up to fair value — died on 8 July 2026. What remains is an ordinary holding-company-discount trade: the shares sit about 8% below the market value of just the Lagardère stake, and roughly 14% below a full look-through value that also credits (a now loss-making) Prisma. That discount is real but *structurally sticky*, because Bolloré-controlled vehicles trade at persistent discounts and control removes any mechanism for minorities to force closure. With the stock near its highs and no forcing function left, the honest classification is dead-money-with-asset-backing, not asymmetric upside.

**Economic moat.** The durable earnings sit inside Lagardère. Publishing (Hachette Livre — the world's third-largest trade-book publisher) has an intangible-brand and backlist moat that is real but narrow; travel retail has scale in airport concessions, but returns are competed away at each concession renewal, so that too is narrow. Group returns on capital look optically low (weighed down by goodwill and lease accounting), but the underlying franchises earn steady, mid-single-digit-growing profits. **Moat: narrow; trend: stable** — recurring profit is rising and margins are steady-to-improving, so this is not an eroding franchise.

**Secular threat.** Manageable, not terminal. Trade-book publishing carries some long-run exposure to generative-AI and e-book substitution, but physical trade books have proven resilient and Hachette's backlist is an asset, not a liability. Travel retail grows structurally with air passenger traffic. Neither business faces a melting terminal value. The cheapness here is a *governance/holding-company discount*, not a fear-print on a shrinking base — which is why it is a fair-value trade rather than either a screaming bargain or a value trap.
